# C23 _BitInt: bit-precise integers beyond fixed widths

After reading this chapter, you will be able to declare signed and unsigned `_BitInt(N)` values, predict `sizeof` packing for common widths, demonstrate wraparound at exact bit width, and choose `_BitInt` over fixed-width types or `__int128` when a protocol or algorithm needs a precise width.

## What `_BitInt(N)` adds

C historically gave you `int`, `long`, and (in C99) `intN_t` / `uintN_t` for 8/16/32/64. Widths like 24, 48, or 127 required bit-fields, manual masking, or compiler extensions such as GCC's `__int128`.

C23 introduces **bit-precise integers**:

```c
_BitInt(24) x;
unsigned _BitInt(48) y;
```

`N` is an integer constant expression with $1 \le N \le \mathtt{BITINT\_MAXWIDTH}$. On GCC 14.2 as verified here, `__BITINT_MAXWIDTH__` is `65535`.

These are real integer types: they participate in arithmetic, usual conversions (with careful rank rules), and `_Generic`. They are **not** the same as struct bit-fields; they are standalone objects with a precise width.

## Lab: sizes, arithmetic, wrap

<!-- file: bitint-lab.c -->
```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("__BITINT_MAXWIDTH__=%d\n", __BITINT_MAXWIDTH__);
    printf("sizeof(_BitInt(8))=%zu\n", sizeof(_BitInt(8)));
    printf("sizeof(_BitInt(63))=%zu\n", sizeof(_BitInt(63)));
    printf("sizeof(_BitInt(64))=%zu\n", sizeof(_BitInt(64)));
    printf("sizeof(_BitInt(65))=%zu\n", sizeof(_BitInt(65)));
    printf("sizeof(_BitInt(128))=%zu\n", sizeof(_BitInt(128)));
    printf("sizeof(unsigned _BitInt(256))=%zu\n",
           sizeof(unsigned _BitInt(256)));
    printf("sizeof(__int128)=%zu\n", sizeof(__int128));

    _BitInt(128) a = ((_BitInt(128))1 << 100) + 42;
    unsigned long long lo =
        (unsigned long long)(unsigned _BitInt(64))a;
    unsigned long long hi =
        (unsigned long long)(unsigned _BitInt(64))(a >> 64);
    printf("a=2^100+42 hi=%llu lo=%llu\n", hi, lo);

    _BitInt(128) prod = a * 3;
    lo = (unsigned long long)(unsigned _BitInt(64))prod;
    hi = (unsigned long long)(unsigned _BitInt(64))(prod >> 64);
    printf("a*3 hi=%llu lo=%llu\n", hi, lo);

    unsigned _BitInt(7) x = 100;
    unsigned _BitInt(7) y = x + 40; /* 140 mod 128 */
    printf("u7 100+40 -> %u (mod 128)\n", (unsigned)y);

    _BitInt(7) s = 63;
    printf("s7 max=63, 63+1=%d\n", (int)((_BitInt(7))(s + 1)));
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra bitint-lab.c -o bitint-lab
./bitint-lab
```

Verified on `gcc (Debian 14.2.0-19) 14.2.0`:

```text
__BITINT_MAXWIDTH__=65535
sizeof(_BitInt(8))=1
sizeof(_BitInt(63))=8
sizeof(_BitInt(64))=8
sizeof(_BitInt(65))=16
sizeof(_BitInt(128))=16
sizeof(unsigned _BitInt(256))=32
sizeof(__int128)=16
a=2^100+42 hi=68719476736 lo=42
a*3 hi=206158430208 lo=126
u7 100+40 -> 12 (mod 128)
s7 max=63, 63+1=-64
```

### Reading the sizes

Storage is rounded up to a whole number of bytes (and then to the ABI's alignment words). `_BitInt(63)` and `_BitInt(64)` both occupy 8 bytes on this target; `_BitInt(65)` jumps to 16. Do not assume `sizeof(_BitInt(N)) * 8 == N` — padding bits may exist beyond the precise width, but the **value** still wraps at $N$ bits.

### Reading the wrap demos

- `unsigned _BitInt(7)` is modulo $2^7 = 128$. $100 + 40 = 140 \equiv 12 \pmod{128}$.
- signed `_BitInt(7)` ranges from $-64$ to $63$ in two's complement. $63 + 1$ wraps to $-64` when converted back to `_BitInt(7)`.

## Versus `__int128` and fixed-width types

| Tool | Width | Portability |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `uint64_t` | Exactly 64 | C99+, everywhere |
| `__int128` | Exactly 128 | GCC/Clang extension |
| `_BitInt(N)` | Any supported $N$ | C23 + recent GCC/Clang |

Use `_BitInt` when the width is part of a specification (24-bit samples, 384-bit field elements) and your toolchain is C23-capable. Prefer `uintN_t` for the classic powers of two when you do not need odd widths. Treat `__int128` as a fine GCC-specific 128-bit type when you do not need C23 portability.

## Literals

C23 adds `wb` / `uwb` suffixes for bit-precise literals. Tooling support varies; the lab above sticks to casts (`(_BitInt(128))1`) which are clear and portable among C23 compilers that implement the type.

## Practical uses

- Protocol fields that are not 8/16/32/64 bits wide.
- Intermediate arithmetic that must wrap at a crypto-sized width without inventing a big-integer library for a single operation.
- Teaching width-sensitive overflow without the packing quirks of struct bit-fields.

Struct bit-fields remain a layout tool for packed records; `_BitInt` is a **value** tool for arithmetic at width $N$.

## Pitfalls

- Compiling without `-std=c23` (or an equivalent) — the keyword will not be available.
- Assuming `printf("%d", bitint)` works for wide `_BitInt` — cast to a known printable type or split into limbs as in the lab.
- Mixing `_BitInt` with `ckd_*` checked-arithmetic macros carelessly — C23 excludes bit-precise integers from some checked helpers; convert to an ordinary integer first when required.
- Shipping `_BitInt` in a public header without documenting the C23 requirement.


## Rank and conversions (practical view)

Bit-precise integers convert to other integer types explicitly with casts. Implicit conversions follow C23's rank rules: a wider ordinary integer may rank above a narrow `_BitInt`, so mixed expressions deserve explicit casts for readability. When in doubt, cast operands to a common `_BitInt(N)` before arithmetic, then cast results out to `uint64_t` limbs for I/O.

### Splitting wide values for printing

`printf` has no standard conversion for arbitrary `_BitInt`. The lab's pattern — cast successive `unsigned _BitInt(64)` windows — scales to 256-bit values by looping over 64-bit limbs. For debugging, prefer hex limbs over decimal.

## ABI and interoperability

Object size and alignment are implementation-defined beyond the requirement to hold $N$ value bits. Passing `_BitInt` across a shared-library boundary requires matching compilers and flags on both sides. For stable C APIs consumed by other languages, export `uint8_t` arrays or fixed `uint64_t` limbs instead of putting `_BitInt` in the public signature.


## Summary

`_BitInt(N)` finally gives C exact-width integers that are not stuck at the traditional sizes. On GCC 14 with `-std=c23`, widths from a few bits to thousands are usable types with predictable wraparound. Use them when the width is the point; keep `uintN_t` for everyday fixed sizes.
